short: The last pagan emperor tried, and failed, to reverse a generation of Christian ascendancy.
full:
On becoming sole emperor in November 361, Julian publicly renounced the Christianity in which he had been raised and set out to restore traditional cult worship. He reopened and funded pagan temples, restored their confiscated endowments, recalled exiled pagan priests to office, and attempted to build a rival pagan priesthood modelled on the church's own charitable and disciplinary structures, drawing on the Neoplatonism he had studied. His edict on education barred Christian teachers from lecturing on classical texts they did not themselves believe.

Julian did not persecute Christians outright, preferring ridicule and administrative disadvantage to violence, and his reign was too short to reverse decades of institutional Christian growth. He was killed in battle against Persia in June 363, and his successor Jovian restored Christian privilege almost immediately. Julian's restoration remained the last serious attempt by an emperor to reverse the empire's turn toward Christianity.
